prompt: What is an ion?

choices.text: An atom or group of atoms with an overall electric charge
An atom with a different number of neutrons than usual
choices.why: That describes an isotope. Neutrons have no charge, so changing their number doesn't make an ion.

choices.text: A neutral group of atoms joined together
choices.why: That describes a molecule. An ion has an overall charge because its protons and electrons don't balance.

choices.text: A compound made of a metal and a nonmetal
choices.why: That describes an ionic compound, which is made of ions. An ion itself is a single charged species.

explanation: When electrons move from one atom to another, species with an overall electric charge form; these are ions. Positive ions are cations, and negative ions are anions.

prompt: How does a neutral atom become a cation?

choices.text: It loses one or more electrons
It gains one or more protons
choices.why: Protons never move from one atom to another. Ions form only when electrons move.

choices.text: It gains one or more electrons
choices.why: Gaining negatively charged electrons gives an overall negative charge, which makes an anion.

choices.text: It loses one or more neutrons
choices.why: Neutrons have no charge, so losing them can't give the atom a charge. Ions form only when electrons move.

explanation: A cation has an overall positive charge. Only electrons move between atoms, so an atom becomes positive by losing electrons, leaving it with more protons than electrons.

prompt: Which of these elements forms anions rather than cations?

choices.why: Hydrogen is not a metal, but it is the one exception among the common cations: it forms H^+.
Silver is a metal, and metals tend to form cations. Silver forms Ag^+.
Rubidium is a metal, and metals tend to form cations. Rubidium forms Rb^+.

explanation: Metals tend to form cations, while nonmetals tend to form anions. Fluorine is a nonmetal; its atoms gain one electron to form the fluoride ion, F^−.

prompt: A nitrogen atom gains three electrons. Which is the correct way to write the ion that forms?

choices.why: The magnitude of the charge is written before the sign, not after it.
Gaining negatively charged electrons gives a negative charge, not a positive one.
A subscript 3 would mean three nitrogen atoms. The magnitude of the charge goes in the superscript, with the sign.

explanation: Gaining three electrons gives an overall charge of 3−. The charge is written as a right superscript with the number before the sign: N^3−, the nitride ion.

prompt: An aluminum atom has 13 protons and 13 electrons. How many electrons does an Al^3+ ion have?
explanation: A 3+ charge means the atom has lost three electrons, while its 13 protons stay put: 13 − 3 = 10 electrons.

prompt: A selenium atom has 34 protons and 34 electrons. How many electrons does a Se^2− ion have?
explanation: A 2− charge means the atom has gained two electrons: 34 + 2 = 36 electrons. The number of protons stays at 34.

prompt: An Fe^3+ ion has 23 electrons. How many protons does it have?
explanation: A 3+ charge means the ion has three more protons than electrons, because the neutral atom lost three electrons. So it has 23 + 3 = 26 protons, the same as a neutral iron atom.

prompt: An ion has 50 protons and 46 electrons. What is its overall charge?

choices.why: There are fewer electrons than protons, so the positive charges win and the ion is positive.
The charge is the difference between the numbers of protons and electrons, not the number of electrons.
That counts only the protons. The 46 electrons cancel 46 of those positive charges.

explanation: Each proton contributes 1+ and each electron 1−. There are 50 − 46 = 4 more protons than electrons, so the charge is 4+: the atom lost four electrons.

prompt: Which is the formula of the sulfite ion?

choices.why: That is sulfate. The -ite ion has one less oxygen atom than the -ate ion.
Sulfite has the same 2− charge as sulfate; only the number of oxygen atoms differs.
That is the sulfide ion, a monatomic ion. The -ite ending belongs to a polyatomic ion that contains oxygen.

explanation: Sulfate is SO4^2−. An -ite ion has one less oxygen atom than the matching -ate ion but the same charge, so sulfite is SO3^2−.

prompt: The chlorate ion is ClO3^−. What is the formula of the chlorite ion?

choices.why: That has one more oxygen atom; it is perchlorate. An -ite ion has one less oxygen atom than the -ate ion.
The number of oxygen atoms is right, but an -ite ion keeps the same charge as the -ate ion: 1−.
The -ite and -ate ions differ in their number of oxygen atoms, not in their charge.

explanation: An -ite ion has one less oxygen atom than the matching -ate ion, with the same charge. Removing one oxygen atom from ClO3^− gives ClO2^−.

prompt: Which of these polyatomic ions is a cation?

choices.why: Acetate, C2H3O2^−, is an anion with a 1− charge.
Cyanide, CN^−, is an anion with a 1− charge.
Bicarbonate, HCO3^−, is an anion with a 1− charge.

explanation: Of the common polyatomic ions, only ammonium, NH4^+, is a cation; the rest are anions.

prompt: Which ion is named correctly?

choices.why: A monatomic anion is named with the stem of the element name plus -ide: the sulfide ion.
Cobalt can form 2+ or 3+ ions, so the name must give the charge: the cobalt(III) ion.
Potassium forms only a 1+ ion, so no Roman numeral is needed: the potassium ion.

explanation: A monatomic anion is named with the element's stem plus -ide, so I^− is the iodide ion. A cation takes the element's name, with a Roman numeral only when the metal can have more than one charge.

prompt: One compound of gold is named gold(III) chloride. What does the (III) in the name tell you?

choices.text: Each gold ion has a 3+ charge
The formula contains three gold ions
choices.why: Ionic names never count ions. The Roman numeral gives the charge on the metal ion.

choices.text: Each gold atom has gained three electrons
choices.why: A positive charge comes from losing electrons. A 3+ gold ion has lost three electrons.

choices.text: Gold can form only a 3+ ion
choices.why: The numeral is needed precisely because gold can form more than one charge: 1+ or 3+.

explanation: When a metal can form more than one charge, the charge goes in the name as a Roman numeral in parentheses. Gold forms 1+ and 3+ ions, and gold(III) means Au^3+.

prompt: A student writes the formula of the ionic compound made of K^+ and S^2− ions as KS. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: The charges don't balance: it needs two K^+ ions for each S^2− ion
The anion should come first, so it should be written SK
choices.why: The cation is always written first in an ionic formula, so K correctly comes first.

choices.text: The charges must be shown, so it should be written K^+S^2−
choices.why: Charges are not written in an ionic formula; they are used only to work out the subscripts.

choices.text: The charges don't balance: it needs two S^2− ions for each K^+ ion
choices.why: Two S^2− ions give 4−, which one K^+ (1+) can't balance. It is potassium that needs a second ion.

explanation: One K^+ (1+) and one S^2− (2−) leave a net 1− charge. Two K^+ ions give 2+, which balances one S^2−, so the formula is K2S.

prompt: Which ionic formula is written correctly?

choices.why: The charges balance, but the convention is to use the lowest ratio of ions: MgO.
One Ca^2+ and one Br^− leave a net 1+ charge. Two bromide ions are needed: CaBr2.
The cation is written first and the anion second: AlCl3.

explanation: Zn3P2 has three Zn^2+ ions (6+) and two P^3− ions (6−), so the charges balance in the lowest ratio, with the cation written first.

prompt: A student writes the formula of the compound of Al^3+ and OH^− ions as AlOH3. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: Without parentheses, the 3 applies only to H
Aluminum should get the subscript, as Al3OH
choices.why: Three Al^3+ ions would give 9+, which one OH^− (1−) can't balance.

choices.text: Polyatomic ions take no subscripts, so it is AlOH
choices.why: AlOH leaves a net 2+ charge. A polyatomic ion can have a subscript when it is written in parentheses.

choices.text: The hydroxide ion should come first, as (OH)3Al
choices.why: The cation is always written first in an ionic formula.

explanation: Three OH^− ions are needed to balance one Al^3+. When more than one polyatomic ion is needed, its formula goes in parentheses with the subscript outside: Al(OH)3. AlOH3 instead reads as one O atom and three H atoms.

prompt: Calcium phosphate is added to some foods as a source of calcium. What is its formula?

choices.why: Without parentheses, the 2 would apply only to oxygen. The subscript for a polyatomic ion goes outside parentheses.
Two Ca^2+ ions give 4+ and three PO4^3− ions give 9−, which don't balance; the subscripts are swapped.
One Ca^2+ (2+) and one PO4^3− (3−) leave a net 1− charge.

explanation: Calcium forms Ca^2+, and phosphate is PO4^3−. The least common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6, so three Ca^2+ ions (6+) balance two PO4^3− ions (6−): Ca3(PO4)2.

prompt: Lead(IV) oxide is used in car batteries. What is its formula?

choices.why: The charges balance, but the convention is to use the lowest ratio of ions.
PbO pairs one Pb^2+ with one O^2−, which is lead(II) oxide. The (IV) means each lead ion is 4+.
The IV is lead's charge, not the number of oxide ions. Four O^2− ions give 8−, but one Pb^4+ gives only 4+.

explanation: Lead(IV) means Pb^4+, and oxide is O^2−. Two O^2− ions (4−) balance one Pb^4+ (4+), so the formula is PbO2.

prompt: Sodium peroxide has been used to bleach wood pulp for making paper. What is its formula?

choices.why: The peroxide ion, O2^2−, is a single unit whose two oxygen atoms can't be split, so the formula isn't reduced to NaO.
Na2O contains the oxide ion, O^2−, so it is sodium oxide. Peroxide is O2^2−.
Peroxide has a 2− charge, so one Na^+ (1+) can't balance it; two Na^+ ions are needed.

explanation: Sodium forms Na^+, and the peroxide ion is O2^2−. Two Na^+ ions balance one O2^2−, giving Na2O2; the 2 on oxygen belongs to the peroxide ion itself and can't be reduced.

prompt: Which pair of ions can combine to form an ionic compound?

choices.why: Both are cations. An ionic compound needs both a cation and an anion.
Both are anions. An ionic compound is never formed from two anions only.
These are two different iron ions, but both are cations, so an anion is still missing.

explanation: A proper ionic formula always has a cation and an anion, never two cations or two anions only. K^+ and Br^− combine one to one as KBr.

prompt: Aluminum sulfate, Al2(SO4)3, is used to purify drinking water. How many ions in total (cations plus anions) does the formula Al2(SO4)3 represent?
explanation: The formula has two Al^3+ ions and three SO4^2− ions (the 3 outside the parentheses counts sulfate ions), for 2 + 3 = 5 ions. The charges balance: 6+ and 6−.

prompt: Suppose a tiny piece of scandium sulfide contains exactly 1,000 Sc^3+ ions. Sulfide ions are S^2−. How many sulfide ions does the piece contain?
explanation: The 1,000 Sc^3+ ions carry a total positive charge of 1,000 × 3 = 3,000, so the sulfide ions must carry 3,000 of negative charge: 3,000 ÷ 2 = 1,500 S^2− ions. This matches the formula Sc2S3, with 3 sulfide ions for every 2 scandium ions.

prompt: Which formula is paired with its correct name?

choices.why: Calcium forms only a 2+ ion, so its compounds take no Roman numeral: calcium oxide.
Ionic compound names don't use numerical prefixes: sodium sulfide.
The anion is named with the element's stem plus -ide: zinc sulfide.

explanation: An ionic compound is named cation first, then anion, with no numerical prefixes. Strontium forms only Sr^2+, so no Roman numeral is needed, and Br^− is bromide.

prompt: SnS2 is a gold-colored ionic compound used as a pigment. What is the charge on each tin ion in SnS2?

choices.why: The 2 counts sulfide ions. Two S^2− ions total 4−, so the one tin ion must be 4+.
No subscript on Sn means there is one tin ion, not that its charge is 1+.
Tin is a metal, so it forms cations. The 4− is the total charge of the two sulfide ions.

explanation: Sulfide is S^2−, so two sulfide ions carry 4−. The single tin ion must balance that with 4+, so SnS2 is tin(IV) sulfide.

prompt: A student names Pb(NO3)2 "lead(III) nitrate." What mistake did the student make?

choices.text: Took the 3 in NO3 as lead's charge; it is lead(II) nitrate
Used a numeral; lead forms one charge, so it is lead nitrate
choices.why: Lead can form 2+ or 4+ ions, so the name needs a Roman numeral.

choices.text: Left out a prefix; two nitrate ions make it lead dinitrate
choices.why: Ionic compound names never use numerical prefixes to count ions.

choices.text: Misnamed the anion; NO3^− is nitrite, so it is lead(III) nitrite
choices.why: NO3^− is nitrate. Nitrite, NO2^−, has one less oxygen atom.

explanation: The 3 in NO3 counts oxygen atoms in the nitrate ion. Two NO3^− ions carry 2−, so the lead ion is 2+, and the name is lead(II) nitrate.

prompt: Ionic compound names don't use numerical prefixes, yet K2Cr2O7 is named potassium dichromate. Why does the name contain di-?

choices.text: Di- is part of the name of the Cr2O7^2− ion itself
Di- counts the two potassium ions in the formula
choices.why: Prefixes are never used to count ions in an ionic name, and if they were, di- would go on potassium.

choices.text: K2Cr2O7 is a molecular compound, so it takes prefixes
choices.why: Potassium is a metal; K2Cr2O7 is made of K^+ and Cr2O7^2− ions, so it is ionic.

choices.text: Prefixes are used whenever a polyatomic ion is present
choices.why: Calcium nitrate, Ca(NO3)2, contains polyatomic ions, yet its name has no prefix.

explanation: The only exception to the no-prefix rule is a polyatomic ion whose own name contains a prefix, such as dichromate, Cr2O7^2−. Potassium dichromate has two K^+ ions and one Cr2O7^2− ion.

prompt: Which of these compounds needs a Roman numeral in its name?

choices.why: Zinc forms only a 2+ ion, so this is simply zinc chloride.
Potassium forms only a 1+ ion, so this is simply potassium chloride.
Aluminum forms only a 3+ ion, so this is simply aluminum bromide.

explanation: A Roman numeral is needed only when the metal can form more than one charge. Nickel forms 2+ and 3+ ions, so NiCl2 is nickel(II) chloride.

prompt: Which of these compounds is molecular rather than ionic?

choices.why: Strontium is a metal, so a compound of strontium and chlorine is ionic.
Scandium is a metal, so a compound of scandium and chlorine is ionic.
Tin is a metal, so a compound of tin and chlorine is ionic.

explanation: Ionic compounds form between metals and nonmetals, while molecular compounds form between nonmetals. Sulfur and chlorine are both nonmetals, so SCl2 (sulfur dichloride) is molecular.

prompt: Which of these compounds is named using numerical prefixes such as di- or penta-?

choices.why: Sodium is a metal, so Na2O is ionic and is named sodium oxide, with no prefixes.
Iron is a metal, so FeBr3 is ionic: iron(III) bromide. Its charge is shown by a Roman numeral, not a prefix.
Calcium is a metal, so CaI2 is ionic and is named calcium iodide, not calcium diiodide.

explanation: Numerical prefixes are used only for molecular compounds, which form between nonmetals. Phosphorus and chlorine are both nonmetals, so PCl5 is phosphorus pentachloride.

prompt: What does the subscript 2 in the ionic formula ZnBr2 tell you?

choices.text: Two Br^− ions balance the charge of one Zn^2+ ion

choices.why: Bromine is present as negatively charged Br^− ions, not as the neutral element, Br2.

choices.text: Each bromide ion has a 2− charge
choices.why: Bromide is Br^−. Subscripts count ions; they don't show charges.

choices.text: There are two zinc ions for each bromide ion
choices.why: A subscript counts the element written just before it, which here is bromine.

explanation: Zinc forms Zn^2+ and bromine forms Br^−, so two bromide ions are needed to balance one zinc ion. The 2 counts bromide ions; elemental bromine is not part of the compound.
